title: Building Energy Model
prompt:
Calculate the peak cooling load and estimate the annual cooling energy consumption for a commercial office building in Phoenix, Arizona (latitude 33.4°N).

Building specifications:
- Floor plan: rectangular, 30 m × 20 m (600 m² per floor), single storey.
- Floor-to-ceiling height: 3.0 m.
- Orientation: long axis runs east-west (30 m facades face north and south, 20 m facades face east and west).
- Window-to-wall ratio: 40% on all facades.
- Glazing: double-pane low-e, U = 1.8 W/(m²·K), SHGC = 0.35.
- Wall construction: insulated metal panel, U = 0.35 W/(m²·K).
- Roof: insulated metal deck, U = 0.25 W/(m²·K).
- Floor: slab-on-grade (ignore floor losses for cooling calculation).

Internal loads:
- Occupancy: 1 person per 10 m² = 60 people. Sensible heat: 75 W/person. Latent heat: 55 W/person.
- Lighting: 10 W/m² = 6000 W total.
- Equipment: 15 W/m² = 9000 W total.

Ventilation:
- Outdoor air: 10 L/s per person = 600 L/s total.
- Phoenix design conditions (ASHRAE 0.4% cooling): dry-bulb 43°C, wet-bulb 21°C (very hot, very dry).
- Indoor conditions: 24°C dry-bulb, 50% RH.

Your calculation must include:

A. SOLAR GAIN CALCULATION:
1. Determine which facade receives peak solar radiation and at what time. For Phoenix in summer:
   - The WEST facade receives peak radiation in the late afternoon (around 3-5 PM solar time) when outdoor temperature is also near maximum. This typically produces the peak cooling load.
   - The SOUTH facade receives less radiation in summer (high sun angle) than in winter.
   - Do NOT apply peak solar irradiance to all facades simultaneously — this is physically impossible. The sun illuminates at most 2-3 facades at any time, and peak irradiance occurs at different times for each facade.
2. For the peak hour, calculate solar gain through windows on each illuminated facade:
   Q_solar = A_window × SHGC × I_solar × SC (shading coefficient, assume 1.0 if no shading specified).
3. Use approximate peak solar irradiance values for Phoenix, 33.4°N, July:
   - West facade at 4 PM: ~700 W/m²
   - South facade at 4 PM: ~250 W/m²
   - East facade at 4 PM: ~0 W/m² (in shadow)
   - North facade at 4 PM: ~50 W/m² (diffuse only)
   - Horizontal (roof): ~800 W/m² at noon, ~500 W/m² at 4 PM (but roof has no windows).

B. ENVELOPE LOADS (at peak hour, outdoor 43°C):
1. Wall conduction: Q_wall = U_wall × A_wall_opaque × (T_out - T_in).
2. Window conduction: Q_window_cond = U_window × A_window × (T_out - T_in).
3. Roof conduction: Q_roof = U_roof × A_roof × (T_out_sol-air - T_in). The sol-air temperature for a dark roof in Phoenix can be 65-75°C.
4. Calculate each component separately.

C. VENTILATION LOADS:
1. Sensible ventilation load: Q_vent_sensible = ṁ × c_p × (T_out - T_in) = ρ × V̇ × c_p × (T_out - T_in).
2. Latent ventilation load: Q_vent_latent = ṁ × h_fg × (ω_out - ω_in), where ω is the humidity ratio.
   - Outdoor: 43°C DB, 21°C WB → ω_out ≈ 0.006 kg/kg (Phoenix is VERY DRY — this is a trap for models that assume humid conditions).
   - Indoor: 24°C, 50% RH → ω_in ≈ 0.009 kg/kg.
   - In Phoenix, ω_out < ω_in, meaning the latent ventilation load is NEGATIVE (outdoor air is drier than indoor air). This reduces the cooling load, it does not add to it.
3. Do NOT double-count ventilation with infiltration unless both are specified separately.

D. INTERNAL LOADS:
1. Sum occupancy sensible + latent, lighting, and equipment loads.

E. PEAK COOLING LOAD:
1. Sum all components: solar + envelope + ventilation (sensible + latent) + internal.
2. Note that the latent ventilation component is negative in Phoenix — subtracting it from the total.
3. Express in kW and in W/m².

F. ANNUAL ENERGY ESTIMATE:
1. Use the degree-day method or bin method for a rough annual estimate.
2. Phoenix cooling degree days (base 18°C): approximately 2500-3000 CDD.
3. Estimate annual cooling energy in kWh, accounting for COP of the cooling system (assume COP = 3.5).

G. SUMMARY TABLE:
Load component | Peak value (kW) | Notes
verification_method: Key checks: (1) Solar gain must NOT be applied to all facades at peak simultaneously. The peak load occurs when the west facade sees maximum radiation (late afternoon) AND outdoor temperature is near maximum. (2) The latent ventilation load in Phoenix is NEGATIVE (ω_out ≈ 0.006 < ω_in ≈ 0.009). Models that add a large positive latent load are wrong. (3) Approximate peak cooling load breakdown: solar gain ~25-30 kW, envelope conduction ~15-20 kW (including sol-air temperature on roof), ventilation sensible ~14 kW, ventilation latent ~ -2 kW (negative!), internal loads ~20 kW. Total peak ~75-85 kW or ~125-140 W/m². (4) Annual cooling energy: roughly 150,000-200,000 kWh thermal, or 43,000-57,000 kWh electrical at COP 3.5.
why_frontier_hard: Three specific failure modes: (1) Applying peak solar irradiance to all four facades simultaneously (physically impossible — the sun cannot be on the east and west facades at the same time). This roughly doubles the solar gain. (2) Adding a large positive latent ventilation load when Phoenix's extremely dry climate (21°C WB at 43°C DB) means outdoor air has LESS moisture than indoor air at 50% RH and 24°C. Models trained on humid-climate examples consistently get this wrong. (3) Double-counting solar gain (once through SHGC on windows, then again as part of sol-air temperature on walls). The sol-air temperature correction applies only to opaque surfaces, not glazing.
